_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and most have a near-miss in another section (Hana's sister vs Kofi's uncle; Isla's hoped-for national squad vs Hana's tournament in Germany; Ewan's calm vs Hana's shaking hands; Isla's small club vs Kofi's growing one). Used by the Part 7 practice page and by Full test 5.
title: Not your usual sport
subtitle: Four young people describe the unusual sports they compete in.

sections.A: Isla, 17, underwater hockey. I'd been a competitive swimmer since I was eight, but when I hurt my shoulder at fourteen, my coach told me to stop racing for at least a year. I was miserable until a friend took me along to an underwater hockey session at our local pool. You play on the bottom of the pool with a short stick and a heavy puck, wearing a mask, snorkel and fins. Because I was already used to swimming lengths, the breath-holding came easily. The hardest part is that you can't shout to your teammates, so you rely on hand signals and on knowing where everyone is likely to be. Our club only has eleven players, which means we sometimes can't enter tournaments because we can't put a full team in the water. I'm hoping to get picked for the national squad next season, though.
sections.B: Kofi, 19, unicycle hockey. My uncle has ridden a unicycle for thirty years, and when I was twelve he gave me his old one and promised to teach me. It took six months of falling off in the back garden before I could ride from one end of it to the other, and only then was I allowed anywhere near a hockey stick. The game itself is a lot like ice hockey, except that everyone is wobbling. You can't touch the ball unless you're properly balanced on the unicycle, which sounds simple until you try it. When I ride to training, people in the street stare or shout things at me, but I've stopped noticing. Our club started with six of us in a borrowed sports hall; there are now nearly forty members, and we've had to book a second evening.
sections.C: Hana, 16, sport stacking. When I tell people I stack plastic cups competitively, they usually laugh and ask if it's a real sport. It is, though: you build and take down pyramids of cups in set patterns, against the clock, and the top stackers do it in under six seconds. My older sister brought a set home from a summer camp, but she lost interest after a month, so I taught myself from videos online. Last year I was chosen to compete for Britain at a tournament in Germany, which was the best and worst weekend of my life. My hands were shaking so much before my first round that I knocked the whole pyramid over. I'd calmed down by my third attempt. Some of the ten-year-olds there were faster than me, which was a bit humbling.
sections.D: Ewan, 18, stone skimming. Almost everyone has skimmed a stone on holiday, but not many people know there's a proper championship every September on a lake near where I live. The rules are strict: stones must be natural and no bigger than a fixed size, and the number of bounces doesn't matter, only the distance. What I love is that I can practise anywhere there's water, and it doesn't cost me a penny. I spend hours on the beach choosing the perfect flat stone. Competitions don't make me nervous at all; there's just you, the stone and the water. The people I really look up to are the men and women in their seventies who've been competing for decades. One woman, who's eighty-one, still throws further than most of the teenagers, and she's always happy to share her tips.

questions.question: Which person turned to this sport when a physical problem forced them to stop another one?
questions.why: 'When I hurt my shoulder at fourteen, my coach told me to stop racing for at least a year.' Kofi fell off often while learning, but was never injured.

questions.question: Which person says that others often doubt whether the activity counts as a proper sport?
questions.why: People 'usually laugh and ask if it's a real sport'. Kofi gets stared at in the street, but nobody questions whether unicycle hockey is a sport.

questions.question: Which person was taught the basics by a relative?
questions.why: His uncle 'gave me his old one and promised to teach me'. Hana's sister brought the cups home, but Hana 'taught myself from videos online'.

questions.question: Which person appreciates being able to train without spending any money?
questions.why: 'I can practise anywhere there's water, and it doesn't cost me a penny.'

questions.question: Which person says players have to find ways of understanding each other without speaking?
questions.why: 'You can't shout to your teammates, so you rely on hand signals.'

questions.question: Which person describes how nerves affected their performance?
questions.why: 'My hands were shaking so much ... that I knocked the whole pyramid over.' Ewan says competitions 'don't make me nervous at all'.

questions.question: Which person needed a long period of practice before they were allowed to play?
questions.why: Six months 'falling off in the back garden', and 'only then was I allowed anywhere near a hockey stick'. Isla found the breath-holding 'came easily'.

questions.question: Which person has already represented their country abroad?
questions.why: 'I was chosen to compete for Britain at a tournament in Germany.' Isla only hopes 'to get picked for the national squad'.

questions.question: Which person says that a lack of players sometimes stops their club from competing?
questions.why: With eleven players 'we sometimes can't enter tournaments'. Kofi's club is the opposite: it has grown to nearly forty.

questions.question: Which person has great respect for some much older competitors?
questions.why: 'The people I really look up to are the men and women in their seventies.' Hana mentions faster ten-year-olds, but they make her feel humble rather than admiring.
